title: Egma
excerpt: Egma Order is Egma's B2B lens ordering platform for optical stores. Creative Navy redesigned the platform across twelve sprints, with case evidence limited to the documented problem, design response, engagement record and evidence boundaries.
metaDescription: Case study of Egma Order, a B2B lens ordering platform redesigned across twelve sprints with explicit evidence limits.
summary: Egma Order is a B2B lens ordering platform used by optical stores to place prescription, stock, bulk stock and service orders. Creative Navy redesigned the web platform, native mobile application and administration area across twelve sprints, supported by research with 17 optometrists across four rounds, five internal stakeholder functions, sandbox domain learning, decision-tree mapping and a delivered design system. The platform is built and online, but no post-launch performance measurement is recorded.

## Egma Order as a B2B lens ordering platform for optical stores

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Egma Order is Egma's B2B lens ordering platform. Egma is a Dubai-based ophthalmic lens manufacturer and optical supplier operating across the Gulf states and North Africa through ophthalmic lenses, eyewear, instruments and a lens factory. Egma's customers are optical stores, including opticians, optometrists and ophthalmologists, who use Egma Order to place lens orders.

Creative Navy redesigned Egma Order across twelve sprints, with a UX phase producing wireframes followed by a UI phase producing the interface and the design system. The Creative Navy-recorded team comprised five people: UX designer, UI designer, interaction designer, researcher and project manager.

Creative Navy-recorded delivery covered 43 screens and 231 screen variants. The distinction matters: 231 refers to distinct screen states, not unique screens. The scope covered the web platform, a native mobile application and the administration area.

Egma Order covers four order types. RX is a prescription order for a named patient and goes into production. Stock covers finished lenses with no production time. Bulk Stock supports store-level replenishment. Services covers fitting, tinting and coating applied to a lens Egma did not make.

## Prescription lens ordering as dependency-constrained configuration

Egma Order addresses a configuration problem in which every selected parameter narrows what remains available. Fitting type governs whether frame data exists. Frame shape governs available diameters. Refraction governs which focal types are producible. Focal type governs technology. Technology governs which individualised parameters are meaningful.

The domain constraint was not general form complexity. Egma's case evidence describes a lens order as a dependency-constrained workflow where a user's earlier selections determine which later selections can exist. Individualised lens technologies require as-worn frame-fit parameters, including corneal vertex distance, pantoscopic tilt, face form angle and inset. Egma's stated position during the engagement was that optimised and individualised lenses can be produced for an uncut lens given the shape, but the individual parameters cannot be collected when there is no frame. The interface therefore needed to explain the absence rather than simply hide the option.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treated this as an expert workflow rather than a novice education problem. Egma stated that the target users were optometrists and opticians who already knew the terminology. The design problem was to make the lens configurator, repeat ordering, order tracking and support flows operable under the conditions in which optical stores use them.

## The legacy Egma Order interface produced late refusal without repair

The documented before state of Egma Order was that users could work partway through a lens order and then be told that the lens could not be produced, without being told which earlier parameter to change. The support team gave a worked example: an optometrist attempted to order reading lenses for a patient, reached a refusal message about the selected shape, could not identify which parameters would allow the intended shape, and created a support ticket instead of completing the order.

That account is a support-team report. It is not a measured failure rate. Its importance is that it identifies the operational workaround: customers asked Egma's support team to place orders on their behalf when the order form did not give a usable repair path.

Five internal functions described the before state differently. Egma's CEO reported that the configurator was restraining revenue because customers did not appear to find the full set of available lens configurations. Egma's product manager reported difficulty with repeat ordering, feature additions and support load. Egma's marketing manager reported weak discovery of premium options, weak branding and no clear user journey. Egma's development team reported that improvement requests arrived as more buttons and content, adding chaos rather than structure. Egma's support team reported customers raising tickets so support staff would place orders for them.

Creative Navy-observed legacy interface details supported those stakeholder accounts. Mandatory inputs were styled in a way that looked like error signalling. Some mandatory inputs sat behind extra clicks. Future order steps were blurred but still legible enough to distract from the current step. A double-layer navigation had been added to compensate for poor discovery of the four order types. Input fields and buttons shared a visual style. The legacy order form presented twelve or more parameter groups on a single screen, with no indication of which choices governed which others.

## Research combined optometrist rounds, stakeholder interviews and domain learning

Creative Navy-recorded research for Egma Order involved 17 optometrists across four rounds: 20-minute structured interviews, 30-minute semi-structured interviews, and two follow-up sessions in which wireframes were shown and feedback was collected. The case evidence does not record whether all 17 optometrists participated in every round, so no participant number is attached to an individual round.

Creative Navy also interviewed internal stakeholders across five functions: Egma's CEO, product manager, marketing manager, development team and support team. The value of those interviews was not simple confirmation. The functions described different versions of the failure, and Creative Navy's triangulation treated the discrepancies as findings in their own right.

Creative Navy's domain learning included hands-on use of the existing configurator in a sandbox environment. That work established the hidden complexity and dependencies between configuration options by using the system rather than only reading about it.

Creative Navy mapped the decision tree before and after the redesign. The before model showed many simultaneously available decision points immediately after login, with crossing paths. The after model resolved to four top-level branches — order lenses, order services, track an order and get support — with mostly linear paths beneath them, so users were not required to make several decisions at once.

Creative Navy and Egma also used a collaborative requirements artefact: a module-by-module table pairing Creative Navy's questions with Egma's written answers, including columns for content and actions, priority, questions, comments and answers. In Creative Navy's vocabulary this is an example of the blanks phenomenon: assumptions had to be written down where they could be inspected, answered and prioritised.

## A heatmap identified hesitation but is not post-launch measurement

A heatmap produced during the engagement identified three regions of the order form where users hesitated: the end of the left-hand column, the two primary actions at the bottom right, and the right-hand technology area, which users passed over. The finding is tool-generated and reflects real behaviour; the capture method is not on record, so it is reported as an observation rather than a measurement.

This heatmap is useful because it located hesitation in the interface where interviews could identify only that users struggled. It is not evidence of post-launch performance. The case evidence does not record the tool, the sample, the conditions, or whether the surface was a prototype or the live platform.

## Creative Navy resolved the dependency problem through availability, explanation, visibility and warned invalidation

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed the Egma Order dependency problem through tension-driven reasoning. Hiding unavailable options reduced clutter, but discoverability mattered because Egma's CEO had reported that customers did not appear to find all available configurations. Showing everything would preserve discovery but reproduce the overloaded interface. The design response was to hide unavailable options while keeping an explanation mechanism that told users why an option was absent and what would need to change for it to become available.

The first move was availability as the primary mechanism. The order form disclosed progressively by dependency. The product, focal type, technology, index, coating and sun protection column remained inert until a fitting type had been chosen, carrying the message that the fitting type needed to be selected first. After that, only producible options were offered, and unavailable options were hidden rather than shown disabled.

The second move was an explicit account of absence. Creative Navy's design position was that missing options should not be silently removed from the user's understanding. The explanation mechanism carried the reason for absence without crowding the main interface with disabled options.

The third move was keeping the whole order visible while the user worked. A multi-step wizard on separate screens was considered and rejected. Because every choice limits later choices, users need to check previous selections constantly. Egma Order therefore shows a same-screen summary of completed sections and allows users to jump back to edit them.

The fourth move was cascade invalidation warned before it happens. When a user edits a completed earlier section, the interface states before the change is committed that subsequent sections will be emptied. The user can apply the change or discard it. This gives the user the cost of the change at the moment of making it, rather than allowing the order to become inconsistent and refusing it later.

## Information and feedback became separate interaction components

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method separated information from feedback after Egma drew a distinction during the engagement. A tooltip explaining what a field means is information: it is static and independent of user input. A message explaining why an option is missing given what the user has chosen is feedback: it is dynamic and responds to entries.

The separation changed the help model. Creative Navy had explored grouped-help alternatives, including section-level definitions and a floating help window. Egma questioned whether this user population needed that level of help and rejected the grouped mechanisms. What shipped was the least obtrusive form: a hover tooltip on text labels.

The hover tooltip decision has an explicit cost in the case evidence. Creative Navy documented that hidden help affects accessibility and goes against conventional UX best practice. The decision was accepted because Egma described the users as experienced optometrists who knew the terminology, making the tooltips a convenience rather than a requirement. The same completion must be stated for mobile: hover help does not exist on the mobile application, and Egma acknowledged that the component is difficult to implement there.

## Bulk ordering, order tracking and tables used progressive specification

Creative Navy's design work on Egma Order used progressive specification where the underlying system was too large or varied to show at once. Bulk ordering, order tracking and table design show the pattern at different scales.

Bulk stock ordering spans approximately 7,000 lens types, client-stated as part of Egma's operating context. Creative Navy made this tractable by offering repeat-a-past-order first, because most stores keep the same few lens types in stock. The next layer was filtering by eight criteria: brand, index, sphere, cylinder, sub-technology, coating, sun protection and diameter. The quantities step then auto-calculates the percentage each lens type represents of the total, and the footer carries a running count of selected lens types and total quantity.

Order tracking was proposed by Egma and resolved by Creative Navy. Egma's revision document described the problem: three order types go into production, and each may require frame or colour-sample collection before production begins. Egma proposed headline states, a current sub-status on hover and the full breakdown on click. The delivered design kept the disclosure mechanism but changed the headline structure to three groups: Order Processed, In Production and Delivery. Those groups span eleven production steps, from order received through delivered. The Orders area is split into drafts, in progress and complete.

The table cell became a design-system component because table content in Egma Order is unusually varied. A single table-cell component absorbed header cells, plain text, clickable tags, input fields, image thumbnails, icon buttons, checkboxes and toggles, each with default, hover and selected states. Supporting table behaviours included a frozen first column with horizontal scroll, drag-to-resize columns, show and hide columns, card-view switching, pagination and bulk delete with select-all and a sticky action bar.

## Access control reattached accountability at committing actions

Egma Order needed fast user switching inside stores without losing personal accountability. Egma specified the model in its revision document: the store logs in, operators switch users without re-entering a password, and a personal code issued through the chain's IT manager is required when an order is placed. Creative Navy extended the code to ticket submission and designed masked and unmasked entry states.

This design reattached accountability at the two committing actions: placing an order and submitting a ticket. It avoided forcing constant re-authentication during rush-hour store work while still recording the individual operator at the point where a transaction or support request is committed.

Egma's administration model is component-based. An administrator creates a role, selects which interface components that role may reach, and sets the access level per component: no access, view or edit. A bulk control sets every permission for a component at once, and individual toggles handle exceptions. Different administrator types see different subsets of administration capability. Stores are view-only in the administration area because store records are maintained in a separate internal system and changes require approval from several departments.

## Mobile design preserved the same ordering task under phone constraints

Creative Navy's mobile design for Egma Order addressed the same ordering task rather than reducing it to a separate simplified product. The mobile application used two input fields per row with steppers so a full prescription for both eyes could fit on a single screen at small resolutions and the keyboard did not have to open. The stepper increment matched the domain unit: 0.25 for dioptres.

Lens shape selection moved into a bottom overlay on mobile. The stated constraint was representational fidelity: showing the shapes inline at phone scale would make them too small to represent the actual lens. The stepper was the only component built for mobile alone. Typography was shared between web and mobile except for headings.

A login screen was also produced at the end of the engagement, outside the UX phase, because Egma asked for it and there had been no time for it earlier. It was added to both the web platform and the mobile app, with the mobile form positioned higher on the screen to sit above the keyboard.

## Declined requests and scoped modules show multi-perspective synthesis

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used multi-perspective synthesis where different business needs conflicted. Egma's marketing team wanted home-page marketing content to open as a pop-up every time the mobile app opened. Creative Navy argued that pop-ups are usually dismissed before their content has been read. The resolution was a top card on the mobile home page with a close control. The close control opens a hide-news menu that deliberately has no permanent-dismiss option, so frequent users are not forced to dismiss the same content every time while marketing retains recurring visibility.

Shade previews were removed from every shade component on web and mobile at Egma's request. Egma's reason was that a simulated shade would not reliably resemble the delivered lens. This is recorded as an Egma-authored decision, not as a Creative Navy preference.

Campaigns were scoped by Creative Navy because Egma stated it had no real business requirements for the campaign module and left the flow to Creative Navy with five constraints. The campaign creation screen lets a marketer set name, priority, start and end dates and content with inline formatting, select chains with select-all and exclusions, review exclusions through a hide-selected toggle, and preview the result as it will appear on the home page. Before this, each campaign required marketing to send content to the development team and wait for implementation.

## The design system handover was taught as operational knowledge

Creative Navy delivered a design system for Egma Order and taught Egma's developers how to operate the design file. The system included typography rules shared between web and mobile except for headings, a small colour palette, corner-radius and shadow rules, a 61-symbol icon set at 20 px from a commercial icon library with the source link retained, the logo as a component, one bespoke homepage illustration, a 4 px spacing grid, responsive breakpoints and a component library covering buttons, inputs, a mobile stepper, navigation, segmented controls, menu items, toast notifications, tags, sliders, cards and table cells.

The final session was training rather than presentation. Creative Navy taught Egma's developers to measure padding and gaps, jump from an instance to its main component, inspect component states, sample colour values, bulk-export icons as SVG and use a plugin that lists every place a component variant has been used. Creative Navy also offered to send the SVGs ahead of the final file and remained reachable in Egma's workspace for implementation questions.

Discarded explorations were retained in the Figma file on purpose, including UI style exploration. This preserved the record of what had been tried so that someone who was not in the room could navigate the reasoning later. In Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, the UX phase mapped to Sandbox Experiments and Concept Convergence, while the UI phase delivered Iterative System Building and reached Organizational Integration through the design system and handover. Implementation Partnership is not claimed for this case.

## Egma Order is online, but the case does not claim post-launch performance outcomes

The platform is built and online. That is a stateable engagement fact. It is not a measured outcome.

No post-launch measurement is recorded for Egma Order. The case evidence contains no support-ticket volume, order completion rate, error rate, average order value, adoption figure or time-on-task result. The before state can be described precisely, and the design response can be described precisely, but the case does not claim that support tickets fell, revenue increased, premium-option discovery improved, or live-platform usability was measured.

At the close of the engagement Egma's CEO described Creative Navy's timeline management as better than that of any third party the company had worked with, and said that Creative Navy always had reasoning behind what it proposed. This is client-reported and unquantified: it is an assessment of the engagement, given before the platform was in use, and it is not a measure of the platform's performance.

Egma commissioned a follow-up engagement on a different product. That is a separate fact about the client relationship. The follow-up material is not evidence about Egma Order, except that Egma's optical expert later independently corroborated Creative Navy's domain learning by describing the difficulty of understanding the optical subject matter.

## Related pages

This case belongs with Creative Navy's Enterprise Software context because Egma Order is a multi-tenant commercial platform with four transaction types, a design-system constraint, support-ticket workflows, an administration area and a permission model.

The heatmap finding belongs with the evidence standard for observations that are not quantified. The engagement record and research programme belong with evidence that was recorded as part of the work, not with outcome claims. The client's assessment of the engagement belongs with client-reported evidence. The absence of post-launch measurement belongs with the page describing what Creative Navy does not claim.

The research structure also relates to Triangulation Not Confirmation. The collaborative requirements artefact parallels documented work in Streetec kntrl 2 and AIT Heat Pump Controller, and the information-versus-feedback distinction belongs near Assemblio as another case where two interface behaviours that looked similar had to be separated because they meant different things operationally.
